# Families of hypotheses and underdetermination in science {#hypotheses}

## Testing theories

Finding things out involves testing hypotheses, but the hypothesis a study can actually measure is rarely the one it cares about. I follow the broad rationalist view that theories are models of some reality that must survive serious testing to count as adequate, and that we learn most from the ways they turn out to be wrong [@Mayo1996; @MayoEa2009]. The difficulty is that a test never confronts a single hypothesis. It confronts a network: the substantive claim of interest, the particular prediction derived from it, and a cushion of auxiliary assumptions that must hold for the derivation and the measurement to go through. When a prediction fails, any node or any link in that network can be blamed. When it succeeds, the success is shared out among all of them. The remainder of this section reconstructs that network for @WalkdenEa2023 and then asks what kind of support a corpus test of a particular hypothesis can really transmit to the substantive theory above it.

The authors are explicit that the substantive target is Trudgill's theory as advertised in @Trudgill2011 and elsewhere (emphasis mine):

> This article is about how to **assess Trudgill's theory** using the most powerful methodological tool that contemporary historical linguistics has at its disposal: the study of the historical record itself, in the form of textual corpora. [@WalkdenEa2023, 546]

## Substantive hypotheses and their auxiliaries

The theory to be evaluated collects *substantive hypotheses*, its *tenets*, such as (among many others):

* Adults learn second languages through a different mechanism than children.
* The adult mechanism leads to simplification, ideally because of spelled-out cognitive principles.
* The social parameters of the contact situation influence the direction and pace of change.
* This yields different temporal scales at which contact-induced change takes place.

Refuting hypotheses this broad is hard. They rest on the aforementioned cushion of *auxiliary hypotheses* that can always absorb an apparent refutation, and they are almost never tested directly, and they have to be broken down into particular hypotheses, which are in turn converted into statistical ones. The boundary between tenet and auxiliary is itself not always sharp. Some auxiliaries any linguist would grant. Others are substantive in their own right. Again, I merely provide some examples of a much larger set of hypotheses that have to be assumed to be true:

* L2 learners may exert linguistic influence on L1 speakers of the same language.
* Language contact can induce change under certain (ideally fully specified) conditions.
* The theory applies universally because it rests on general cognitive and/or social principles.
* "*Population-level patterns are not entirely random and [...] individuals' usage can be non-categorical but still pattern meaningfully in probabilistic ways*" [@WalkdenEa2023, 549] --- a strong and very specific assumption.
* The loss of number inflection on pre-nominal elements is simplification.
* The addition of pronominal subjects in a predominantly pro-drop language is simplification.
* The move from synthetic case inflection to adpositional marking is simplification.

## Particular hypotheses and their auxiliaries

The authors then introduce the historical corpus-based approach as suited to collecting evidence for the theory, which adds a further tier of assumptions about the method's applicability. Because the theory makes *predictions*, they derive *particular hypotheses*. These cannot themselves be tenets, or they would not be predictions. The approach is avowedly confirmatory --- the studies are offered as *support* (emphasis mine):

> In **support of our approach**, we present three case studies of morphosyntactic phenomena for which the theory of sociolinguistic typology makes predictions, and assess them using historical corpus evidence. [The three case studies] taken together [illustrate] how historical corpus evidence can be brought to bear on questions of sociolinguistic typology. [@WalkdenEa2023, 547]

From this and the earlier quote we can deduce that the authors are in fact explicitly trying to achieve two things at once: test Trudgill's theory and verify that their method provides adequate means for doing so.
It is not made explicit which of the two neighbourhoods of the network of hypotheses (the methodological or the deep-theory neighbourhood) would be identified as the source of the error in case the test failed.
Some concrete particular hypotheses concern the diachronic development of:

* the loss of number marking on pre-nominal elements in English under Norse contact (Section \@ref(study1));
* the rise of overtly expressed pronominal subjects in Latin American Spanish under contact with enslaved Africans who acquired Spanish as adults (Section \@ref(study2));
* the reorganisation of case and adposition systems in the diffuse contact situation of the Balkan sprachbund.

Each carries its own *auxiliary hypotheses* of measurement and operationalisation --- not derived from the theory but required for the procedure to mean anything, for example:

* The mechanisms posited by the theory are mirrored reliably, and with negligible delay, in the written record.
* The surviving sources are rich and faithful enough to register subtle diachronic change.
* The change observed is due largely to contact, and not to general tendencies of change that happen to fall in the same place and time.
* The authors of the texts were connected enough to the speech community to be good exponents of the change, rather than silent monks or ivory-tower writers.

## Underdetermination, and why it matters in linguistics

A successful test using corpus data is supposed to transmit support upward, from the particular hypothesis to the substantive theory, by treating every auxiliary as true. But the auxiliaries are not innocent. Any false one can manufacture a pseudo-confirmation. The method may be inadequate to the surviving sources, the loss of pre-nominal inflection may not be "simplification" in any relevant sense, Trudgill's theory may simply be wrong. The advertised reading holds only if the auxiliaries are *true to a satisfying degree* --- not merely *plausible*, since plausibility measures our belief, and the validity of the inference does not turn on what we believe.

This is the classical problem of the underdetermination of theory by data, and it comes in two forms that compound here. Its *holistic* form is the familiar Duhem--Quine point that a refutation falls on the whole conjunction of hypotheses, not the one under test --- the form already built into the network of Section \@ref(hypotheses) [@Duhem1914; @Quine1951]. @Laudan1990 argued that this was overstated as in mature sciences we can usually localise the blame and repair the network. That reply is fair where theories make precise predictions, which is exactly where linguistics (including the present case and much of my own work) is substantially different from the examples Laudan probably had in mind.

*Contrastive* underdetermination compounds the problem. A set of theories is contrastively underdetermined when the data are compatible with all of them, and nothing in the data breaks the tie. @LaudanLapplin1991 dismissed this on the grounds that two genuine rivals will seldom draw exactly equal support from the same evidence. Their argument, though, presupposes that the rivals make claims precise enough for "more" and "less" support to be measured. However, linguistic theories more often than not do not make such precise claims. Many of them are largely informal and pre-numerical (which does not mean they could never make such precise predictions), so the evidence cannot be apportioned between rivals in the first place. Consider Study 1 (Section \@ref(study1)): the loss of plural marking on every NP element but the head noun is compatible with Norse contact and with the well-known general drift of English away from inflection from Old to Early Modern English, which might have accidentally progressed faster in the Northern regions than in the Southern ones. A North-to-South progression during the Danelaw would tip the balance toward the contact account --- but only somewhat, and the data remain compatible with both. There is no numerical prediction sharp enough in current theories to break the tie decisively.

This is what I mean by the loose fit of informal theory to data, and it is the common root of both forms. Holistic underdetermination keeps a failed prediction from refuting the theory, because the blame can always fall on an auxiliary. Contrastive underdetermination keeps a successful one from confirming it, because a rival is compatible with the same result. The imprecision of the theory is what allows each to operate. A circle can be drawn around any figure, if it is large enough. The practical consequence is that, for substantive linguistic hypotheses, we can secure neither confirmation nor refutation. The most a corpus study like the ones we routinely run can deliver is that the data either fail to contradict the conjunction of our hypotheses (which is not confirmation) or fail to be compatible with it (which, given the loose fit, is not clean refutation either).

The asymmetry with the mature sciences is stark. I invite the reader to name one major linguistic theory of the last thirty-odd years that was abandoned because it stood in clear, repeated, demonstrated conflict with data. Theories have gone out of fashion, but that is not the same thing. Compare Newton's gravitation, ultimately broken by the anomalous precession of Mercury's perihelion [@Leverrier1859]: the numbers from the theory and the numbers from observation did not match, and there was no way around it. Linguistics, as of today, rarely affords numbers that unforgiving. Keeping this in view is essential for the next section, where I turn to what statistics can and cannot add to the testing of such hypotheses.

## Statistical hypotheses and severe testing {#testing}

For quantitative work, the particular hypotheses of the previous section must be turned into *statistical hypotheses*: expectations about a numerical outcome of counting or measuring. Given the low degree of formalisation, that outcome is usually as imprecise as "$n$ should be greater than $m$." For the loss of number marking on pre-nominal elements under Norse contact, for instance, we might expect inflected pre-nominal elements to occur less often in Northern and Eastern dialects than in Southern and Western ones during the Danelaw. Call this $H_1$: "*Occurrence counts of inflected pre-nominal elements are lower in the North and East than in the South and West.*"

This is where matters more often than not get confusing. It is statistically far easier to check a sample for (unusually substantial) *divergence* from a hypothesis than for *accordance* with it, so the hypothesis is inverted into a *Null*, $H_0$, and frequentist theory gives the probability of obtaining a sample at least as extreme as the observed one if the Null were true --- the p-value. A low p-value (by convention usually $p<0.05$) is then read as licence to infer $H_1$, which, if we read the previous sentence carefully, it is not.
That approach to statistical inference is called Null-Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST), and it has been under heavy fire for two decades, almost unnoticed in linguistics.^[A marginal but real debate about significance testing in corpus linguistics does exist [for example, @Kilgarriff2005; @Koplenig2019].]
Several aspects of NHST inference are outright invalid [@Gigerenzer2004; @GreenlandEa2016; @Mayo2018], and I only name three. 
First and most devastatingly, the incompatibility of a single set of data with a rather uninformative negation of a statistical hypothesis cannot be taken as corroboration, let alone proof of that hypothesis.
A vast number of alternatives to the Null are compatible with the data if $p<0.05$, and the test does not strongly predicate anything about the statistical hypothesis of interest and next to nothing about the complex network of hypotheses it came from. 
Second, the p-value is only a good approximation of the actual probability if the probability distribution underlying the observed phenomenon is both known and appropriate for the test, which is almost never the case, especially in corpus linguistics.
In more complex models (see below), this extends to a requirement that the model be specified correctly with all sources of variance accounted for at the right place (informally speaking) within the model, and in the correct form.
Third, a p-value threshold of 0.05 tolerates, in the long run and under the Null, one false alarm in twenty.
In many cases such a low bar seems rather cavalier, especially as sample sizes rise and the test becomes ever more sensitive to minute effects (see below).
These issues and many more arise from the fact that NHST is an unstable hybrid of two incompatible inferential philosophies, Fisher's significance testing and the Neyman--Pearson theory of decisions between hypotheses, welded into a procedure neither founder would endorse [see @Lehmann2011 for a historical deep dive].

Deborah Mayo's *severity* requirement makes the deeper problem underlying statistical confusion such as in NHST precise [@Mayo1996; @MayoSpanos2004; @Mayo2018]. In its weak form: *data do not provide good evidence for a hypothesis if they come from a procedure with very little capacity to have detected the hypothesis's falsity, had it been false* [paraphrased from @MayoSpanos2004, 162]. A hypothesis earns the label *corroborated* only by surviving many tests with a real chance of exposing its potential falsehood. Reading a single low p-value, derived from one Null, as corroboration of the whole network of substantive and particular hypotheses behind it (Section \@ref(hypotheses)) is a flagrant breach of that requirement: such a test has almost no capacity to detect errors in the hypotheses that actually matter.

It is crucial to keep in mind that *any* real divergence, however slight, makes the Null technically false. Even with moderate sample sizes, NHST detects this easily by throwing a low p-value. Suppose the effect posited in Study 1 held for one ten-thousandth of speakers. The Null would then be technically false, NHST would flag it given a large enough sample (or simply an unlucky one containing a text or two from those few speakers), and the result could be paraded as corroboration of Trudgill's theory. It would be nothing of the kind: no severe test was performed, and a discrepancy that small tells us nothing about English under the Danelaw. This is also the mechanism behind the loose fit of Section \@ref(hypotheses): a low-severity test is precisely how an informal, underdetermined theory manufactures the confirmation I argued it could never legitimately earn. The fault is not in frequentist inference but in this use of it.

Many of the deficiencies I document below stem from this adherence to NHST. I will argue in Section \@ref(gooduse) that a few straightforward practices would have forestalled most of them.
Among those practices are a careful, bias-resistant inspection of one's own models, reviewers equipped to catch inferential and statistical errors, and relief from the pressure to report only positive findings. I do not suspect the authors of dredging or negligence. I am confident they acted in good faith, having seen the same confusions in many other researchers and in my own earlier work. But the field suffers if papers like @WalkdenEa2023 pass without methodological scrutiny.
